titre: The Cleaver, the Suffragette, and the Venus at Her Mirror
accroche: In 1914, a militant slashes with a cleaver the only female nude painted by Velázquez, and gives two different reasons for her act, almost 40 years apart.
contenu_vulgarise:
On March 10, 1914, an elegant woman walks into the National Gallery in London and stops in front of Velázquez's *Rokeby Venus* (known in French as *La Vénus au miroir*), the only female nude by Velázquez to have come down to us. She has hidden a meat cleaver under her coat. In a few seconds, she lands seven blows on the canvas, slashing the figure's back between the shoulder blades, before the guards overpower her.

The woman is Mary Richardson. She is a member of the Women's Social and Political Union, the suffragist movement led by Emmeline Pankhurst. She writes a statement to the WSPU on the spot, published the next day in The Times: she wanted to destroy what the government considers the most valuable thing in the country, in protest against its way of destroying Mrs Pankhurst, arrested the day before. The painting, bought eight years earlier by the National Art Collections Fund for the National Gallery, becomes in her act the symbolic equivalent of a woman's body that the state lets waste away in prison.

## The Mechanism

Richardson had already burned down, with her accomplice Jane Short, a historic manor house in Hampton, The Elms; she was one of the first two women subjected to force-feeding after the Cat and Mouse Act of 1913 came into force. The choice of a painting rather than a building is no accident: it strikes a public institution without endangering any life, and it guarantees immediate press coverage. Richardson is tried and sentenced to six months in prison, the maximum sentence then provided for destroying a work of art.

## What It Shifts

Almost 40 years later, in 1952, Richardson gives a different reason for her act, in an interview: she says she disliked the way male visitors stood in front of the painting all day long. The two explanations do not necessarily contradict each other, but they do not put the emphasis in the same place: an immediate political protest against a comrade's imprisonment, or an older unease at the gaze directed at a woman's body painted by a man. Nothing makes it possible to decide which of the two really guided her hand that day, or whether one simply seemed more presentable than the other depending on the era in which she was asked.

The painting, restored by the National Gallery's chief conservator, Helmut Ruhemann, returned to the galleries. The scars remain visible to those who know where to look. On November 6, 2023, activists from the Just Stop Oil movement damaged the same canvas again, smashing its protective glass with hammers to demand an end to new oil and gas licenses in the United Kingdom: more than a century later, painting remains the surface on which people come to inscribe a cause that has nothing to do with it.

repere.texte: Richardson lands seven cleaver blows on the canvas and is sentenced to six months in prison, the maximum sentence then provided for destroying a work of art; the restored painting returns to the galleries of the National Gallery.

carte.punch: On March 10, 1914, a suffragette slashes with a cleaver the only female nude painted by Velázquez.
carte.idee: Mary Richardson slashes Velázquez's Venus at Her Mirror seven times to protest the arrest of Emmeline Pankhurst the day before. Decades later, she would give another reason for her act: the gaze of men on this painting.

quiz.question: Why does Mary Richardson target this particular painting on March 10, 1914?
choix: To protest the record price paid by the National Gallery to acquire it
Because the police had just arrested Emmeline Pankhurst, and she wanted to draw a parallel between the two
Because no woman painter was displayed in the same galleries of the museum
To prevent the sale of the painting to a collector living abroad
quiz.explication: Richardson states at the time that she is protesting the arrest of Emmeline Pankhurst the day before; the purchase price, the absence of women painters, and a sale abroad are not among the reasons she gives then.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What weapon does Mary Richardson use to attack the painting, and how many blows does she land?
choix: A kitchen knife, for three quick blows
An ax hidden in a bag, for a single powerful blow
A hammer, for five blows on the painting's frame
A meat cleaver hidden under her coat, for seven blows
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says she hid a meat cleaver under her coat and landed seven blows on the canvas in a few seconds.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What had Mary Richardson done before her attack on the Velázquez painting, according to the text?
choix: She had already vandalized another painting at the National Gallery
She had burned down, with Jane Short, the historic manor house of The Elms in Hampton
She had organized a demonstration in front of the British Parliament
She had been jailed for shoplifting
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says she had already burned down, with her accomplice Jane Short, the historic manor house of The Elms in Hampton.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What other reason does Mary Richardson give for her act, decades later, in 1952?
choix: She says she hated the gaze of the men who stood in front of the painting all day long
She says she wanted to protest the purchase price the museum paid for the painting
She says she acted on Emmeline Pankhurst's direct orders
She says she wanted to draw attention to her own work as a painter
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says that in 1952, Richardson explains that she disliked the way male visitors stood in front of the painting.
